lead: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pushes out in one minute. Doctors need it to judge whether a sick heart is pumping enough, and to guide drugs and fluids. Dilution methods measure it without opening the chest: inject a known amount of indicator into the blood, then record how the indicator concentration changes downstream. The faster the blood flows, the more the indicator is spread out and the smaller the concentration peak becomes. This chapter covers two hospital standards: dye dilution with indocyanine green, and thermal dilution with cold saline through a pulmonary artery catheter.
prereq: You need: the heart rate and cardiac cycle ideas from Unit 1, and the transducer and bio-amplifier basics from Unit 1; the pressure measurement in 2.1 shows the same idea of a sensor on a catheter.

sections.h3: Cardiac output and the dilution principle

blocks.text: Cardiac output (CO) is the blood volume the heart ejects per minute, in litres per minute (L/min). At rest an adult heart moves about 5 L/min; during exercise it can rise several times. CO = heart rate × stroke volume, but measuring stroke volume directly is hard, so dilution methods infer the flow from how blood carries an injected indicator.

The Fick principle is the reference method: oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference gives CO. It needs blood gas analysis, covered in Unit 3. Dilution methods use the same conservation idea with an indicator instead of oxygen.

Inject a known mass I (mg) of indicator into a vein. Downstream, a sensor records concentration c(t) in mg/L against time t in seconds. If blood flow is Q in L/s and the indicator mixes completely, then I = Q ∫ c(t) dt. The integral A = ∫ c(t) dt has units mg·s/L and is the area under the concentration-time curve. Rearranged and converted to minutes:

blocks.where: CO is cardiac output in L/min; I is the mass of indicator injected in mg; A = ∫ c(t) dt is the area under the first-pass concentration-time curve in mg·s/L; 60 converts seconds to minutes.

blocks.text: The method assumes complete mixing, no indicator loss before the sensor, and steady flow during the measurement. Those assumptions are the reason the recording technique matters.

Dye dilution uses indocyanine green (ICG), a green dye that stays in the blood vessels and is removed by the liver. A typical dose is 5 mg, injected rapidly into a central vein. Arterial blood is drawn through a densitometer, a small cuvette that measures light absorption at the dye's wavelength. The recorder plots dye concentration against time. The curve rises as the first bolus passes the sampling site, peaks within a few seconds, then falls.

After about 20–30 s some dye returns through the circulation and creates a second, smaller hump called recirculation. That hump is not part of the first pass. To find the true first-pass area, plot the falling part of the curve on semilog paper, fit a straight line, and extend it below the recirculation hump. The area under the first-pass curve — the measured part plus the extrapolated part — is A. Equivalently, take the area under the original curve up to the start of recirculation, then add the area under the extrapolated line from that time onward.

items: Inject a known mass I of ICG into a central vein.
Draw arterial blood through a densitometer and record c(t) for 30–40 s.
Identify the first-pass peak and the start of recirculation.
Extrapolate the downslope on semilog paper to remove the recirculation hump.
Measure A by planimetry or by numerical integration.

blocks.text: ICG is relatively safe, but it contains iodine, so allergy matters. The method is accurate when the curve is clean. The area is what matters; the height alone is not CO.

sections.h3: Thermal dilution and the Swan-Ganz catheter

blocks.text: Thermal dilution replaces the dye with cold fluid and the densitometer with a thermistor. A Swan-Ganz catheter floats through the right heart into the pulmonary artery. It has a proximal port in the right atrium and a thermistor near its tip in the pulmonary artery. A known volume, commonly 10 mL, of cold saline or dextrose is injected into the right atrium. The thermistor records the small fall and recovery of blood temperature as the cold bolus passes.
The recorder plots temperature change ΔT (°C) against time (s). The area under this curve, A<sub>T</sub> = ∫ ΔT dt, has units °C·s. The monitor computes:

blocks.where: CO is cardiac output in L/min; A<sub>T</sub> = ∫ ΔT dt is the area under the temperature-time curve in °C·s; K is the computation constant supplied with the catheter, in the units the monitor expects.

blocks.text: K bundles the injectate volume, its specific heat and density, the blood temperature, and catheter factors. Enter the correct K for the injectate volume and temperature; a wrong K gives a wrong CO even when the curve is perfect.

Iced injectate (0–4 °C) gives a larger temperature difference from blood, so a larger ΔT and a better signal-to-noise ratio. Room-temperature injectate is also used and is more comfortable, but the constant changes. Thermal dilution is safer than dye: no dye reaction, no liver clearance problem, and it can be repeated every few minutes. The main risks are those of the catheter itself, not the indicator.

figure.caption: The dye concentration rises sharply after injection and falls almost exponentially; the area under this first-pass curve is A in CO = 60 I/A. In a real recording a small recirculation hump follows and is removed by extrapolating the downslope.

spec.aria: The dye concentration rises sharply after injection and decays almost exponentially; the area under this first-pass curve is the denominator of the Stewart-Hamilton equation.

examples.question: 5 mg of indocyanine green is injected and the arterial concentration curve is recorded. The computed area under the first pass is 60 mg·s/L. (a) Find the cardiac output. (b) What would it be if the area were 50 mg·s/L?
steps: Write the Stewart-Hamilton equation: CO = 60 I / A.
For part (a), substitute I = 5 mg and A = 60 mg·s/L. Check units: mg ÷ (mg·s/L) = L/s; multiplying by 60 s/min gives L/min.
For part (b), keep I = 5 mg and use A = 50 mg·s/L.
A smaller area means the blood carried the dye away faster, so the cardiac output is higher.
examples.answer: (a) The cardiac output is 5 L/min. (b) With a first-pass area of 50 mg·s/L, the cardiac output is 6 L/min.
examples.check:
I = 5.0
A1 = 60.0
CO1 = 60 * I / A1
A2 = 50.0
CO2 = 60 * I / A2
print(CO1)
print(CO2)

traps: Dropping the factor 60 in CO = 60 I / A. With I = 5 mg and A = 60 mg·s/L, dropping 60 gives 0.083 L/s (not L/min), which is the same as 5 L/min.
Including the recirculation hump in A. That makes A too large and CO too small, because CO is inversely proportional to the area.
Mixing time units: the area must be in mg·s/L before multiplying by 60. If the curve is integrated in mg·min/L, do not multiply by 60 again.
Using the wrong computation constant K for thermal dilution when the injectate volume or temperature is changed. The curve can be correct while CO is wrong.
Confusing the dye curve, with concentration in mg/L, and the thermal curve, with temperature change in °C. Their areas have different units and different constants.

quiz.q: Define cardiac output and give a typical resting value for an adult.
quiz.a: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart ejects per minute, in L/min. A typical resting adult value is about 5 L/min.

quiz.q: Which indicator is used in dye dilution, and what sensor measures it in the arterial line?
quiz.a: Indocyanine green is used, and a densitometer measures its light absorption in arterial blood.

quiz.q: Why is the downslope of the dye curve extrapolated before the area is measured?
quiz.a: The downslope is extrapolated to remove the recirculation hump. Otherwise the second pass of dye would be counted in A, making A too large and the calculated CO too small.

quiz.q: Why does iced injectate improve the thermal dilution signal?
quiz.a: Iced injectate gives a larger temperature difference between injectate and blood, so the thermistor sees a larger ΔT. The signal is bigger compared with baseline noise.

quiz.q: 2.5 mg of dye is injected and the first-pass area is 30 mg·s/L. Find the cardiac output.
A patient has cardiac output 4 L/min and 5 mg of dye is injected. What first-pass area would the dye curve give?
quiz.a: Rearrange CO = 60 I / A to A = 60 I / CO = 60 × 5 / 4 = 75 mg·s/L.

quiz.q: A thermal dilution measurement uses 5 mL of injectate, but the monitor's computation constant K is set for 10 mL. The temperature-time curve is valid. What does the monitor report?
quiz.a: The monitor computes CO = K / A_T. A K for 10 mL is larger than the correct K for 5 mL, so the reported CO is too high, roughly by the ratio of the two constants. The curve A_T itself is still valid; the operator must enter the correct K.

quiz.q: Give two reasons thermal dilution is often preferred over dye dilution for repeated bedside measurements.
quiz.a: Cold saline or dextrose is not a dye, so there is no dye allergy or liver-clearance problem, and no toxic accumulation. The measurement can be repeated every few minutes with a Swan-Ganz catheter already in place, using cheap sterile fluid and a thermistor.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern intensive care often estimates cardiac output from arterial pulse contour analysis calibrated by transpulmonary thermodilution, or from lithium dilution. Echocardiography and Doppler ultrasound now give non-invasive estimates and are often used first. Search for 'PiCCO', 'LiDCO', and 'pulse contour cardiac output' for the next layer. A blood cell counter appears beside this topic in some lists; it belongs to Unit 3.
